generatedProse.concept-context: In practice, the same idea is often named in several ways, so a single keyword will miss relevant work. One field may call a group 'teenagers' where another calls them 'adolescents' or 'young people'. Pulling the core concepts out of a question, and listing the alternative terms for each, is how a search reaches the work that one word alone would skip.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two students who need sources for the same question, and both go to search.

Student A types the whole question into the box, word for word. The tool treats common words such as 'does' and 'affect' as search terms, and the results are a scattered mix. Student A has used a sentence where keywords were needed.

Student B pulls out the core concepts first, then lists the alternatives for each. Where one concept might be named two or three ways, all of those terms go on the list. The results come back focused and relevant.

Both searched the same question. Student B searched with concepts and synonyms, while Student A searched with a sentence.
generatedProse.summary: Keywords drive a search, and the same concept is often named in several ways across the literature of any field. You build a set by pulling the core concepts from your question and listing the alternatives for each. You can now assemble a working keyword set of your own. The next lesson combines these terms into a real search.

check.body: In the worked example, why did Student B list alternatives such as 'teenagers' alongside 'adolescents'?

items.text: So the search catches relevant work that uses a different word for the same idea.

feedback.correct: That's right. The literature names the same idea in different ways, so synonyms stop the search missing relevant work.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Think about what a single word would miss when a field names the same idea differently.
